BRIEF

Write an analytical article of about 2,600 words in the house style of the UK Office for National Statistics, bringing together evidence on how UK businesses have adopted and used AI over the period from late 2023 to mid-2026. Give it a plain descriptive title of your own.

Primary source: the Business Insights and Conditions Survey (BICS), Wave 159 (5 to 28 June 2026), with a time series of AI questions running back to September 2023, and the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (May to June 2026) for individual-level AI use. Cover: the trend in the share of businesses using at least one AI technology since late 2023 and variation by business size; the depth of adoption (number of AI technologies used, extent of use, share of employees using AI); variation by industry; comparison of employee-reported and business-reported use; the purposes AI is used for, by size band; how businesses acquire AI (free software, purchased software, in-house, outsourced); reported effects on workforce headcount, overall and by purpose of use; which job roles are affected by which AI technologies; barriers to adoption; and how businesses integrate AI skills. Set the UK figures against international evidence on adoption gaps between the US and Europe and against executive-survey measures of firm adoption, explaining why estimates differ by measurement approach. Refer to other UK government evidence on adoption motivations, management practices and innovation where relevant.

Structure with numbered sections: 1. Main points (five bullets); 2. Background; 3. Use of artificial intelligence in UK businesses; 4. Purpose and impacts of artificial intelligence use; 5. Adoption of artificial intelligence and factors limiting its use. Refer to figures by number with a figure title, a subtitle describing the measure, a "Source:" line and numbered "Notes:". Neutral, impersonal ONS tone ("we" for ONS); no policy recommendations; flag where questions are new and results are early indications.

SOURCES

The materials below are the sources available to you for this piece: the evidence and data the piece should be built from, and the literature it may cite. Where the sources include a data appendix, treat its figures as the results of the analysis the brief describes and report them as you see fit. Cite the sources by name in the citation style the brief specifies. You may also draw on your general knowledge, but every figure you state must come from the sources. Do not invent survey figures. Target length: 2600 words.

===== SOURCE FILE: sources/04_ons/data_appendix_04.txt =====
Data appendix for brief 04 (ONS BICS Wave 159, 5–28 June 2026, businesses with 10+ employees unless stated; OPN 6 May–28 June 2026. Interpretation removed.)

Adoption over time (share of businesses using at least one AI technology): Sept–Oct 2023 ~12%; June 2026 ~35%.
By size, June 2026: 0–9 employees 28%; 250+ employees 49%.
Average number of AI technologies per adopting business: ~1.4 (Sept 2023) to ~1.6 (June 2026).
Technology types used, June 2026 (share of businesses): large language models 18%; visual content creation 16%; data processing using machine learning 12%; image processing using machine learning 6%; robotics 2%; other AI 2%.
Extent of use among adopters: 10% report using AI extensively (0–9 employees 17%; 250+ employees 9%). 15% of businesses report more than half of employees use AI in daily work. Larger businesses more often "not sure" on both measures (new questions this wave).
By industry: information and communication 58% (almost three-fifths) use at least one AI technology; private-sector education also high; construction 13%. Higher-adoption industries also report more multiple-technology use.
Employee vs business: 55% of employed/self-employed report using AI for work or education (OPN, GB) vs 35% of businesses (BICS, UK).
Purpose of use: improving business operations ~60% of businesses (slightly lower among smaller businesses; over 60% of larger businesses); providing/personalising products or services second (31% of 0–9 employee businesses); developing new products/services and exploring new markets lower, and more common among smaller businesses.
Adoption method: free-to-use software most common in manufacturing, wholesale and retail, accommodation and food, administrative and support services; purchased external software or ready-to-use services more common in construction, information and communication, professional/scientific/technical.
Headcount impact: around half of businesses report no impact across size bands (highest among 10–249 employees); just under 7% of medium-sized businesses report a decrease; small businesses slightly lower; a notable share "not sure"/"not applicable".
Among businesses using AI to improve operations: 63% no change; 1% increased headcount; 6% decreased headcount (~6% decrease vs smaller share for other purposes).
Roles affected by technology type: visual content creation → creative/design roles, over half of users; image processing → 53% report impacts on administrative/clerical roles and 53% on creative/design roles; ML data processing → administrative/clerical 41%, data analysis 39%.
Barriers (last three months): 41% report no barriers; lack of expertise ~18% among 100–249 employee businesses; cost 7%–14% across size bands; employee concerns, regulation, product availability less frequently reported.
Skills integration: among businesses citing lack of expertise, 62% train/retrain existing staff vs 26% among those reporting no barriers; businesses with no barriers slightly more likely to automate/replace roles. Overall: training/retraining most common (~40% of medium-to-large businesses); ~10% automate or replace roles; recruiting AI-skilled staff ~2% (smallest) to 10% (250+). 11% of businesses report more than half of workforce has received AI-related training.
External comparators quoted: US workers using generative AI for work early 2026, 43%; UK workers ~36% (St. Louis Fed / NBER "Mind the Gap"); executives' surveys: ~78% of US firms and ~71% of UK firms use at least one AI technology ("Firm Data on AI"); DSIT AI Adoption Research 2026: efficiency/productivity most-cited motivation; ONS 2023 management practices article: barriers = identifying use cases, cost, expertise; BoE DMP Jan 2026: most firms report no material AI impact on employee numbers over past three years.

## S2. Bick, Blandin, Deming, Fuchs-Schündeln & Jessen (2026) — "Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S.", NBER WP 34995 (Mar 2026) [Q]
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w34995 · St. Louis Fed summary (30 Mar 2026): https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2026/mar/mind-gap-ai-adoption-europe-us · IZA DP 18521: https://docs.iza.org/dp18521.pdf
Abstract: "This paper combines international evidence from worker and firm surveys conducted in 2025 and 2026 to document large gaps in AI adoption, both between the US and Europe and across European countries. Cross-country differences in worker demographics and firm composition account for an important share of these gaps. AI adoption, within and across countries, is also closely linked to firm personnel management practices and whether firms actively encourage AI use by workers. Micro-level evidence suggests that AI generates meaningful time savings for many workers. At the macro level, in recent years industries with higher AI adoption rates have experienced faster productivity growth. While we do not establish causality, this relationship is statistically significant and similar in magnitude in Europe and the US. We do not find clear evidence that industry-level AI adoption is associated with employment changes. We discuss limitations of existing data and outline priorities for future data collection to better assess the productivity and labor market effects of AI."

## S3. Yotzov, Barrero, Bloom, Bunn, Davis et al. (2026) — "Firm Data on AI", NBER WP 34836 (Feb 2026) [Q]
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w34836 · PDF: https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w34836/w34836.pdf
Abstract: "We survey nearly 6,000 senior business executives at US, UK, German, and Australian firms to develop new evidence on AI adoption and its effects on jobs, productivity, and output. Specifically, we ask executives about AI usage, its effects at their own firms over the past three years and, looking ahead, what they anticipate over the next three years. We find four main results. First, 69% of firms actively use AI, with higher usage rates at younger and more productive firms. Second, more than two thirds of executives regularly use AI, but their usage rate averages only 1.5 hours a week. Third, executives report little own-firm impact of AI over the last 3 years, with nine-in-ten reporting no impact on employment or productivity. Fourth, these same executives predict sizable effects over the next 3 years, predicting that AI will boost productivity at their firms by an average of 1.4%, raise output 0.8%, and cut employment 0.7%. In contrast, employees anticipate that AI will raise employment 0.5% at their firms in the next 3 years, highlighting an expectations gap between employers and employees."
